Q — Evaluate Locke as the father of liberalism through his two contracts, natural rights, labour theory of property and toleration; and contrast with Hobbes on how each legitimizes state authority.
Locke’s state of nature is peaceful but ‘inconvenient’ (no impartial judge), so people set up government.
They make TWO contracts and transfer only limited powers — creating a limited, ‘trust’ state (unlike Hobbes’ absolute one).
Natural rights to life, liberty and property are inalienable; property comes from mixing one’s labour with nature.
So Hobbes justifies an absolute state, Locke a limited constitutional state with a right to revolt — the birth of liberalism.

Q — Assess Mill’s harm principle and defence of free expression, his status as a ‘reluctant democrat’, and his case for the equality of women, within his revision of utilitarianism. (UPSC 2014/2018/2021)
Mill revised utilitarianism by adding quality — ‘better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’.
His ‘harm principle’: the state may restrict a person only to prevent harm to others.
He fiercely defended free speech — ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’.
A ‘reluctant democrat’, he feared the ‘tyranny of the majority’; and (with Harriet Taylor) he championed women’s equality.

Mill gives liberty priority: ‘over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign’. His
holds that ‘the sole end for which mankind is warranted in interfering with the liberty of a person is to prevent harm to others’ — distinguishing self-regarding from other-regarding action.

‘All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’ — even one dissentient must be heard, for the silenced opinion may be true, or contain part of the truth; hence his defence of the ‘crank’ whose rare genius benefits mankind.

Mill is the ‘first serious liberal democrat’ (Macpherson) — balancing utility with liberty, majority rule with minority rights, and pioneering the case for women’s equality — even if Barker faults his self-/other-regarding distinction as a ‘prophet of empty liberty’.

Q — Discuss Marx’s base-superstructure model, class and class struggle, and alienation; and how Gramsci’s concepts of hegemony, the integral state and organic intellectuals rescued Marxism from economic determinism. (UPSC 2015/2016/2020 + Gramsci 2013/2016/2019)

contentText:
Syllabus — Western Political Thought: Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, John S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci, Hannah Arendt. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 10)







Unit Snapshot

What this unit covers: the canon of Western political thinkers — Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, J.S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci and Hannah Arendt — their central ideas, the comparisons the syllabus draws (Plato vs Aristotle, Hobbes vs Locke, Marx vs Gramsci) and their critiques.

Must-know anchors: Plato (justice, philosopher-king, Popper critique), Aristotle (constitutions, revolution), Machiavelli (realism, virtu-fortuna), Hobbes (Leviathan, sovereignty), Locke (natural rights, limited state), Mill (liberty, harm principle), Marx (materialism, alienation, surplus value), Gramsci (hegemony), Arendt (vita activa, banality of evil).

PYQ trend: Plato/Popper (2015), Aristotle (2015/2017/2019/2021), Machiavelli (2014/2018), Hobbes (2017), Mill (2014/2018/2021), Marx (2015/2016/2020), Gramsci (2013/2015/2016/2019), Arendt (2019).

Master Questions







Q — Examine Plato’s conception of justice, education, communism and the philosopher-king, and evaluate Popper’s charge that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’. (UPSC 2015)





Gist — the spine to recall





Plato’s justice = each class doing its own job (rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce) in harmony.



Education creates this ideal state; rulers are wise ‘philosopher-kings’ who alone should rule.



Communism of property and wives (for rulers & guardians only) removes selfish temptations.



Popper attacks all this as totalitarian — an ‘enemy of the open society’ who froze change and freedom.





Model Answer

For Plato (in The Republic) justice is ‘each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only’ — a functional harmony mirroring the three parts of the soul (reason, spirit, appetite) and the three classes (rulers, guardians, producers) of the ‘myth of the metals’. ‘Justice is the architectonic principle’ and ‘the state is the individual writ large’.

Education and the philosopher-king. Justice is realised through state-sponsored education, a lifelong sieve that culminates, at 50, in the rule of the philosopher-king — ‘until philosophers are rulers or rulers learn philosophy, there is no end to the ills of states’. ‘It is foolish to limit an expert physician with the book of medicine’ — so the philosopher-king rules by wisdom, not law.

Communism. To free the guardians from private temptation, Plato prescribes communism of property and wives — but only for the two ruling classes — an ‘economic solution to a political ailment’ (unlike Marx’s economy-wide, economically-motivated communism).

Popper’s critique. Karl Popper (in The Open Society and Its Enemies) charges that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’ — his rigid class order, censorship and rule by an unaccountable elite amount to totalitarianism, freezing change (‘arrest all political change; change is evil, rest divine’). Bertrand Russell too ‘dubbed Plato a totalitarian’.

Conclusion. Popper’s charge is powerful but arguably anachronistic — defenders like Levinson hold that ‘fascism and Platonism are incomparable’. Whatever the verdict, as Whitehead said, all Western philosophy is ‘footnotes to Plato’ — his linkage of knowledge, virtue and rule remains the founding statement of political philosophy.







Q — Analyse Aristotle’s critique of Plato’s idealism, and contrast their theories of justice and the state. (UPSC 2019)





Gist — the spine to recall





Aristotle, Plato’s student, replaced his teacher’s idealism with realism — ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’.



He rejected Plato’s ‘one man, one job’ justice and his communism as impractical and against human nature.



Plato’s justice is inner/moral (duties); Aristotle’s is external/legal (proportionate, rights-based).



Both see the state as key to the good life, but Plato idealises it while Aristotle studies it empirically.





Model Answer

Aristotle, Plato’s pupil for twenty years, ‘rectified the limitations of Plato’s ideas’ by replacing idealism with empirical realism — ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’ (Will Durant: ‘as Brutus loved Rome more, so for Aristotle dear is Plato, but dearer is truth’).

The critique of idealism. Aristotle rejected Plato’s theory of Forms (a separate ‘world of ideas’) as unreal; his justice of ‘one man, one job’ makes life ‘monotonous’, is too subjective/moral rather than legal, and stresses duties over rights. He attacked Plato’s communism of wives and property: ‘what is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — ‘everyone’s property is no one’s responsibility’ — and defended the family as a ‘time-tested institution’ of emotional stability.

Justice contrasted. For Plato justice is inner, moral and spiritual (harmony of the soul, duties); for Aristotle it is external, legal and practical — ‘proportionate equality’: ‘it is unjust to treat equals unequally and unequals equally’, divided into distributive and corrective justice.

The state contrasted. Both hold the state essential to the good life (Plato: ‘the greatest happiness of the whole’; Aristotle: ‘man is by nature a political animal’, the state exists ‘for the sake of the good life’). But Plato is the idealist/perfectionist designing an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings, whereas Aristotle is the pragmatic realist who studied 158 constitutions and preferred the rule of law and a middle-class ‘polity’.

Conclusion. Aristotle’s realism corrects Plato’s idealism — from an ideal to be constructed to institutions to be studied and improved — which is why he, not Plato, is called the ‘father of political science’, even as both remain rooted in the shared Socratic conviction that the state exists for human excellence.







Q — Explain Aristotle’s classification of constitutions, his theory of proportionate equality and revolution, and assess his contribution to modern constitutional democracy. (UPSC 2021/2017)





Gist — the spine to recall





Aristotle classified governments by how many rule and whether they rule for the common good.



Six types: correct (kingship, aristocracy, polity) and their perverted forms (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy).



‘Polity’ (rule of the many via the middle class) is the golden mean and the most stable.



Revolution springs from a sense of inequality ‘real or imagined’; his ideas feed modern rule of law and constitutionalism.





Model Answer

Aristotle, the ‘father of comparative politics’ who studied 158 constitutions, classified governments on two axes — the number of rulers and whether they rule for the common good or self-interest.

Six-fold classification: rule by one — Kingship (correct) vs Tyranny (perverted); by few — Aristocracy vs Oligarchy; by many — Polity vs Democracy. Polity — the ‘golden mean’ identified with the middle class — is the most stable and practicable, since the middle class moderates the conflict of rich and poor.

Proportionate equality. Justice requires ‘treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’ — proportionate, not absolute, equality, the basis of distributive justice.

Revolution. ‘The feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’, and ‘poverty is the parent of revolution and crime’. Aristotle catalogued the general and regime-specific causes and cures of revolution, counselling moderation and the strengthening of the middle class — a conservative concern for stability.

Contribution to modern democracy. His insistence on the rule of law over the rule of persons (‘law is reason without passion’), the mixed/middle-class polity, and constitutional stability directly anticipate modern constitutional democracy — though his exclusion of women, workers and slaves from citizenship is ‘unacceptable in modern times’.

Conclusion. Aristotle’s empirical, moderate and law-centred vision — government for the common good, balanced by the middle class and bound by law — is the classical seed of modern constitutional democracy, even as its citizenship must be democratised to meet modern standards of equality.







Q — Critically examine Machiavelli’s separation of politics from ethics and religion, and his place in the evolution of political science. (UPSC 2018/2014)





Gist — the spine to recall





Machiavelli separated politics from morality and religion — the first to justify ‘dirty hands’ for the state’s sake.



He judged rulers by success, not virtue: a prince must ‘know how to be bad’ and combine the lion and the fox.



Religion is useful as a tool of discipline — ‘use religion, don’t get used by it’.



By studying politics as it IS (empirically), he became the ‘father of political realism/modern political science’.





Model Answer

Machiavelli, writing in The Prince, founded political realism by divorcing politics from ethics and religion and judging action by its results, not its morality — the first to justify ‘dirty hands’ in statecraft.

Politics vs ethics. Given a selfish human nature (‘men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’), the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad rather than good’ and must combine ‘the courage of the lion with the cunning of the fox’, changing colours ‘like a chameleon’. On the safer bet: ‘it is better for a prince to be feared than loved’.

Politics vs religion. Machiavelli treats religion instrumentally — as a disciplinary, unifying force: the ruler should ‘use religion rather than get used by it’. This makes him, for the text, the ‘father of European secularism’.

Place in political science. By applying the empirical method to human affairs — studying states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’ — Machiavelli marks a decisive break from medieval theology. Ernst Cassirer called him ‘the Galileo of politics’, and ‘if Machiavelli was Copernicus, Hobbes was the Galileo of political theory’.

Critique. He is condemned as ‘the most universally reprobated figure’ (Maxey), an amoral cynic; Sabine finds him ‘narrowly dated and narrowly located’ in Renaissance Italy, and Gandhi saw the separation of ethics from politics as a ‘death trap’.

Conclusion. Whatever the moral verdict, Machiavelli’s realism and empiricism made politics an autonomous, observable domain — which is why, despite universal condemnation, ‘everyone practises Machiavellism without confessing it’ (Dunning), and he stands at the threshold of modern political science.







Q — Discuss Hobbes’ derivation of the state from human nature and the state of nature, his theory of absolute sovereignty and political obligation, and compare him with Machiavelli. (UPSC 2017)





Gist — the spine to recall





Hobbes starts from a selfish, fearful human nature with an ‘endless desire for power’.



Without a state, life is a ‘war of all against all’ — ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’.



So people make ONE contract surrendering all rights to an absolute sovereign (the Leviathan) — obligation is total and irrevocable.



Like Machiavelli he is a realist, but Hobbes builds a systematic theory of sovereignty, not just advice to a prince.





Model Answer

Hobbes, using the ‘resolutive-compositive’ method, derives the state logically from human nature: man has an ‘endless desire for power after power that ceases only in death’ — he is selfish, materialistic and driven by fear (‘fear and I were born twins’).

State of nature. Absent a common power, this produces a ‘war of every man against every man’, where life is ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’, driven by competition, diffidence and glory.

The contract and sovereignty. To escape it, men make a single contract, each with every other, surrendering all their natural rights to a ‘common power’ — creating society and state at once. The resulting sovereign (Leviathan) is ‘absolute, indivisible, inalienable and perpetual’; ‘law is the command of the sovereign’ (anticipating Austin), and ‘covenants without the sword are but words’.

Political obligation. Because the covenant is made among the subjects (not with the sovereign), obligation to obey is total and irrevocable — yet it is grounded in consent for self-preservation, so the one right that cannot be surrendered is the right to life; if the sovereign cannot protect it, obligation lapses.

Hobbes vs Machiavelli. Both are realists who reject classical natural sociability and a moralised politics. But Machiavelli offers practical advice to a prince whose goal is glory, while Hobbes builds a systematic, deductive theory whose goal is escape from the state of nature through absolute sovereignty.

Conclusion. Hobbes converts Machiavellian realism into a rigorous science of the state. Macpherson reads him as the ‘scholar of possessive individualism’ whose theory fits a ‘possessive market society’ — yet by grounding the state in consent and self-preservation, Hobbes is also, paradoxically, a father of modern individualism.







Q — Evaluate Locke as the father of liberalism through his two contracts, natural rights, labour theory of property and toleration; and contrast with Hobbes on how each legitimizes state authority.





Gist — the spine to recall





Locke’s state of nature is peaceful but ‘inconvenient’ (no impartial judge), so people set up government.



They make TWO contracts and transfer only limited powers — creating a limited, ‘trust’ state (unlike Hobbes’ absolute one).



Natural rights to life, liberty and property are inalienable; property comes from mixing one’s labour with nature.



So Hobbes justifies an absolute state, Locke a limited constitutional state with a right to revolt — the birth of liberalism.





Model Answer

Locke, the ‘father of liberalism’, begins from a balanced human nature — reason guides man ‘not to harm others in their life, liberty and property’. His state of nature is ‘a state of peace and mutual assistance’, pre-political but not pre-social, flawed only by two ‘inconveniences’ (men judge in their own case; may act in passion).

Two contracts and the limited state. Men make two contracts — one forming civil society, another forming a government by consent — and transfer only the powers to make, execute and adjudicate law. The state thus holds delegated (trust) power, not original power: a ‘night-watchman’ state whose ‘sole purpose is the protection of property’, with separation of powers (legislative supreme, executive, federative) and a right of revolution against a government that betrays its trust.

Property and toleration. By the labour theory, ‘property is the product of one’s labour’, subject to limits (no spoilage, enough left for others). His Letter Concerning Toleration defends freedom of conscience — though, notably, not for atheists.

Hobbes vs Locke. Both use contract, but from opposite premises: Hobbes — a war-like state of nature, single contract, no natural rights retained, an absolute sovereign, ‘liberty where the law is silent’; Locke — a peaceful state of nature, two contracts, inalienable natural rights, a limited state, ‘no law, no liberty’.

Conclusion. Where Hobbes legitimizes state authority as absolute (to escape chaos), Locke legitimizes it as limited and accountable (to secure pre-existing rights) — which is why Locke, the ‘individualist out and out’, founds the liberal-constitutional tradition that runs through to Rawls.







Q — Assess Mill’s harm principle and defence of free expression, his status as a ‘reluctant democrat’, and his case for the equality of women, within his revision of utilitarianism. (UPSC 2014/2018/2021)





Gist — the spine to recall





Mill revised utilitarianism by adding quality — ‘better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’.



His ‘harm principle’: the state may restrict a person only to prevent harm to others.



He fiercely defended free speech — ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’.



A ‘reluctant democrat’, he feared the ‘tyranny of the majority’; and (with Harriet Taylor) he championed women’s equality.





Model Answer

Mill revised utilitarianism by adding a qualitative dimension — ‘it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’ — rescuing it from Bentham’s ‘pig’s philosophy’.

Liberty and the harm principle. Mill gives liberty priority: ‘over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign’. His harm principle holds that ‘the sole end for which mankind is warranted in interfering with the liberty of a person is to prevent harm to others’ — distinguishing self-regarding from other-regarding action.

Free expression. ‘All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’ — even one dissentient must be heard, for the silenced opinion may be true, or contain part of the truth; hence his defence of the ‘crank’ whose rare genius benefits mankind.

A reluctant democrat. C.L. Wayper calls Mill a ‘reluctant democrat’: fearing the tyranny of the majority (a danger Tocqueville had diagnosed in Democracy in America), Mill proposed safeguards — plural/weighted voting, proportional representation and a strong second chamber — favouring quality over mere numbers.

Subjection of women. In The Subjection of Women (influenced by Harriet Taylor), Mill attacked the legal subordination of women as ‘one of the chief hindrances to human improvement’ — ‘there remains no legal slave save the mistress of every house’ — and argued equality would end the family as ‘a school of despotism’ and ‘double the mass of mental faculties’; he supported women’s suffrage.

Conclusion. Mill is the ‘first serious liberal democrat’ (Macpherson) — balancing utility with liberty, majority rule with minority rights, and pioneering the case for women’s equality — even if Barker faults his self-/other-regarding distinction as a ‘prophet of empty liberty’.







Q — Discuss Marx’s base-superstructure model, class and class struggle, and alienation; and how Gramsci’s concepts of hegemony, the integral state and organic intellectuals rescued Marxism from economic determinism. (UPSC 2015/2016/2020 + Gramsci 2013/2016/2019)





Gist — the spine to recall





Marx: the economic ‘base’ (who owns production) shapes the whole ‘superstructure’ (law, politics, ideas).



History is class struggle; capitalism exploits via surplus value and alienates the worker from his work, product and self.



Gramsci asked why revolution failed — answer: the ruling class rules by ‘hegemony’ (consent), not just force.



So Gramsci gave the superstructure autonomy — rescuing Marxism from crude economic determinism.





Model Answer

For Marx, historical materialism holds that the economic base (mode of production) determines the superstructure: ‘in order to think we must live, to live we must eat, and to eat we must produce’. History advances through class conflict — ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’ — across stages from slave to feudal to capitalist to communist.

Class, surplus value, alienation. Capitalism exploits the worker through surplus value (labour alone creates value; the capitalist pockets the unpaid surplus), and alienates him at four levels — from the process of production, the product, his social nature and himself. When the ‘class in itself’ becomes a ‘class for itself’, revolution follows and the state ‘withers away’.

The problem. Marx’s prediction of revolution in advanced capitalist states failed — exposing the limits of treating the superstructure as a mere ‘reflection’ of the base (the charge of economic determinism).

Gramsci’s rescue. Gramsci, the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, gave it autonomy. The ruling class rules by hegemony — manufacturing consent through civil society (the consent-wing of the ‘integral state’, alongside coercive political society) so that the exploited accept their exploitation as ‘common sense’. Revolution therefore needs a war of position — an ideological battle led by organic intellectuals — before the ‘war of manoeuvre’.

Conclusion. Gramsci shifts the decisive struggle from economics to culture and consciousness, explaining capitalism’s durability and rescuing Marxism from determinism — the pivot from classical Marxism to the neo-Marxist analysis of ideology and hegemony.







Q — Critically examine Arendt’s conceptual triad of labour, work and action, her distinction between power and violence, and her conception of ‘the political’ as the antidote to totalitarianism. (UPSC 2019)





Gist — the spine to recall





Arendt splits human activity into labour (survival), work (making things) and action (public life among equals).



Action is the highest — it makes us truly human (‘zoon politikon’) through speech and plurality.



Power ≠ violence: power is people ‘acting in concert’; violence destroys power but can never create it.



Genuine political action and participation are the antidote to totalitarianism (and to the ‘banality of evil’).





Model Answer

In The Human Condition, Arendt distinguishes the vita activa into three: Labour (the animal laborans — biological necessity, where man is unfree), Work (the homo faber — making durable things), and Action (the highest — public interaction among equals).

Only action, with its two components freedom and plurality, makes man a zoon politikon: through speech and deed among others we disclose who we are and begin something new (‘natality’). Modernity inverts this — the ‘victory of animal laborans over zoon politikon’, the ‘rise of the social’ and ‘world alienation’ — crowding out genuine action.

Power vs violence. ‘Power corresponds to the human ability not just to act but to act in concert’; it ‘belongs to a group and exists only so long as the group holds together’. It is sharply distinct from violence: ‘where genuine power is absent, violence may emerge to fill the gap’, and ‘violence can destroy power but is utterly incapable of creating it’.

The political as antidote to totalitarianism. Totalitarianism (ideology + terror) destroys the plural public realm and reduces men to isolated, thoughtless functionaries — hence the banality of evil (Eichmann in Jerusalem): evil done ‘because of the absence of sound thinking and judgment’. The remedy is a revival of civic republicanism — active participation in a genuine political public sphere.

Conclusion. Arendt relocates freedom from the private/economic realm to the public realm of action, making participation the essence of politics and the safeguard against totalitarianism. Critics (Benhabib, feminists, Marxists) fault her rigid public/private divide for delegitimising material and economic justice — yet her warning that thoughtlessness enables evil remains profound.
